papers.what_it_is: A theory paper proposing to repurpose random circuit sampling quantum supremacy experiments as a certified randomness protocol, with soundness proofs under a hardness assumption and in the random oracle model.

existing.note: The bound is conditional and probabilistic. Theorem 2.1 and Corollary 5.9 give min-entropy of at least B/2 with probability at least (bq minus 1)/(b minus 1) minus a vanishing term over the challenge circuit, for a polynomial-time quantum device that passes LXEB with probability q, and only if the Long List Hardness Assumption holds for parameter B (B is below n/2 because of Grover search). The paper proves that assumption only relative to a random oracle. The worked example (B = 0.49n, b = 1.002, q at least 0.9990) gives about 0.12n bits, so the abstract's Omega(n) hides a small constant.
existing.value: The authors state that, if the Long List Hardness Assumption holds with parameter B for a circuit distribution and a polynomial-time quantum algorithm solves the Linear Cross-Entropy Benchmark with threshold b and probability at least q, then with probability at least (bq minus one) over (b minus one), minus a vanishing term, over the challenge circuit the algorithm's output has min-entropy at least B/2; the worked example with B equal to 0.49n gives at least 0.12n random bits.

existing.value: The authors state they prove the protocol sound in two senses: under a hardness assumption called Long List Quantum Supremacy Verification, which they justify in the random oracle model; and unconditionally in the random oracle model against an eavesdropper who could share arbitrary entanglement with the device, for a device that makes at most two to the power n over 7 queries to a Haar-random circuit. They state they can currently prove security against an entangled adversary only in the random oracle model.

assertions.value: The authors describe the protocol: a classical verifier uses a small random seed to generate challenge circuits pseudorandomly and sends them one at a time to a quantum computer server, which must respond quickly, in less than one second, with independent samples from each circuit's output distribution; the verifier computes the Linear Cross-Entropy Benchmark for at least some circuits and, if the scores are large, is confident under plausible computational assumptions of genuine min-entropy in the samples.
quotes: In our protocol, a classical verifier uses a small random seed to generate n-qubit challenge circuits C1, C2, . . . pseudorandomly.
For each Ci, the server needs to respond quickly—say, in less than one second—with independent samples

If the LXEB scores are sufficiently large, our analysis shows that the verifier can then be confident, under plausible computational assumptions, that there must be Ω(n) bits of genuine min-entropy in the returned samples.
assertions.certainty_reason: The protocol is the paper's own stated setup in Section 1.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that, assuming the returned samples pass the benchmark, the last step of the protocol feeds them into a classical seeded randomness extractor to produce output bits that are exponentially close in total variation distance to uniformly random.

assertions.value: The authors argue that spoofing must be continual and as fast as the quantum computer, while verification can be occasional: the verifier can spot-check a constant number of random rounds, so that a malicious server spoofing even 10 percent of the rounds would be caught with overwhelming probability, and verification can be done after the fact.

assertions.value: The authors state that the protocol has a forward secrecy property: even if the verifier's pseudorandom generator is broken in the future, so long as the server cannot break it when the protocol is run, the server is forced to generate truly random bits.

papers.what_it_is: A theory paper on whether parameterized quantum models can compute all gradients at a cost proportional to one function evaluation, with a lower bound, an algorithm based on shadow tomography, and hardness results.

existing.note: Repeated in Theorem 9 (classical cost of M times two to the power of order n, when no effective approximation scheme is known), in Section 5.2 (removing the cost needs a breakthrough in shadow tomography) and in Appendix D (naive storage of the hypothesis state costs M times two to the power O(n)).

The proved lower bound (Proposition 3) covers only the quantum data setting with no quantum memory (single-copy measurements), where about 2 to the n over epsilon squared copies are needed. The paper says this bound does not carry over to the simplified case where the state is the all-zero state, nor to pure states made by polynomial-size circuits: there the task is information-theoretically possible with classical shadows (Proposition 16). For those cases the paper gives only a computational-hardness argument (Proposition 17, relative to cloning pseudo-random states). The abstract's wording, impossible without multiple copies, is wider than the proved result. The word argue also marks Appendix C.2 as an argument, not a theorem.
existing.value: The authors prove that backpropagation scaling is not possible in general for quantum data when only single copies are measured and there is no quantum memory, using a lower bound on the number of copies needed to predict all Pauli observables. They state that this information-theoretic separation does not generalize to the simplified case of the all-zero initial state or to pure states generated by polynomial-size circuits, and for those they argue that no efficient procedure can exist in the most general case unless pseudo-random quantum states can be efficiently cloned.
